newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk contractors want Libya jobs despite debts.
newsitem.headline: Turk contractors want Libya jobs despite debts.

text.p: Turkish contractors said on Thursday they wanted new projects in Libya despite Tripoli's unpaid debts of more than $300 million and its leader's recent outburst against Turkey.
"We do not want to lose this market," Kadir Sever, head of the Turkish Contractors' Association (TMB), told Reuters
"There is still some work to do there," he said of giant construction projects worth a total of $8.6 billion since Turkish contractors began work in Libya in the early 1970s.

Turkey's Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan this week returned from a controversial trip to Libya, during which Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi severely criticised Turkey's treatment of the Kurds and accused it of being a Western stooge.

Erbakan's silence subjected him to harsh rebukes from the opposition, now gearing up to try and topple him. Washington also criticised him for supporting Libya against Western charges that Tripoli backs terrorism.
But Turkish contractors said they would not like to see the big Libyan market sacrificed for political reasons.

Few foreign leaders have visited Libya since the United Nations slapped a limited embargo on Tripoli in 1991 for its refusal to hand over two Libyans suspected of blowing up a Pan Am airliner in Scotland in 1988.
But Erbakan's predecessor -- Tansu Ciller, leader of the coalition's conservative True Path Party partner -- also visited Libya in 1994 when she was prime minister.
"Gaddafi's comments should not cut off economic and trade ties between the two countries. He has made similar comments before. Political and economic relations should not be mixed," Sever said.
He said Libya offered Turkish contractors new prospects over the next five years, including 60,000 housing units and 10,000 classrooms.
"We cannot undertake these jobs worth $2 billion unless we are backed by the (Turkish) government," he said of the government's diplomatic support in having Libya pay its debts.
Libya's debts due to the contractors from projects completed years ago amount up to $365 million, of which contractors said $120 million was due in 1994 but never paid.

"During the prime minister's visit, $40 million of this amount was decided to be paid immediately, with the remaining to be paid in monthly instalments of $4 million," said Barlas Turan, who represents Turkish contractors in Libya.
Sever blamed the delay in the payment of Libyan debts on previous Turkish governments' lack of attention.

The Association's 19 members have undertaken 257 infrastructure projects in Libya, including housing compounds, dams, roads, water plants and schools since the 1970s. Smaller companies were also involved in deals worth about $3 billion.

According to TMB data, projects worth $1.6 billion have been left unfinished because Libya's reluctance to pay the contractors. "We have to finish off those projects in order to win new contracts," Turan said.
